title: Newton-Girard Identities: Historical Context and Mathlib Infrastructure
content:
The module docstring states the open question and answer: prove the Newton-Girard recurrence $p_k = (-1)^{k+1} k e_k - \sum_{0 < j < k} (-1)^j e_j p_{k-j}$ connecting power sums $p_k = \sum x_i^k$ to elementary symmetric polynomials $e_k$. The import `Mathlib` brings in `MvPolynomial.psum_eq_mul_esymm_sub_sum` — the general recurrence proved in Mathlib — which this file instantiates at $k=1,2,3$. The variable declaration `(σ : Type*) (R : Type*) [CommRing R] [Fintype σ]` establishes the type-generic setting: $\sigma$ is the index type (the variables $x_i$ range over $\sigma$), and the ring $R$ can be any commutative ring.

Newton-Girard identities were first proved by Albert Girard in *Invention nouvelle en l'algèbre* (1629) and independently by Newton around 1666 (published in *Arithmetica Universalis*, 1707). Mathlib formalizes the full recurrence via Zeilberger's combinatorial proof (Bruijn's lattice path interpretation). This file reduces the general recurrence to three explicit corollaries.
mathContext: Power sums and elementary symmetric polynomials in Lean: `psum σ R k = ∑ i : σ, X i ^ k` (the multivariate polynomial $\sum x_i^k$); `esymm σ R k = ∑ s ∈ powersetCard k Finset.univ, ∏ i ∈ s, X i` (the $k$-th elementary symmetric polynomial $e_k$). The general recurrence: $p_k = (-1)^{k+1} k e_k - \sum_{(a,b) \in \text{antidiag}(k),\, 0 < a < k} (-1)^a e_a p_b$.

title: k=1 Corollary: p₁ = e₁ via Mathlib Transitivity
content:
The simplest Newton-Girard identity is $p_1 = e_1$: the first power sum (sum of variables) equals the first elementary symmetric polynomial. In Lean, this requires bridging two separate Mathlib lemmas: `MvPolynomial.psum_one` states $p_1 = \sum_i X_i$ and `MvPolynomial.esymm_one` states $e_1 = \sum_i X_i$. Both equal the same thing, so transitivity (`Eq.trans`) gives $p_1 = e_1$. The proof is a one-liner: `(MvPolynomial.psum_one σ R).trans (MvPolynomial.esymm_one σ R).symm`.

This illustrates a common pattern in Mathlib proofs: two lemmas independently computing the same expression via different definitions, joined by `.trans` and `.symm`. The `.symm` reverses the second equality direction ($\sum X_i = e_1$ becomes $e_1 = \sum X_i$, then transitivity gives $p_1 = e_1$).
mathContext: $p_1 = \sum_{i : \sigma} X_i = e_1$. Lean: `(MvPolynomial.psum_one σ R).trans (MvPolynomial.esymm_one σ R).symm`. The general Newton-Girard recurrence at $k=1$ gives $p_1 = (-1)^2 \cdot 1 \cdot e_1 - 0 = e_1$ (no antidiagonal terms since $0 < j < 1$ is empty).
prerequisites: psum and esymm definitions in MvPolynomial

title: k=2 Corollary: Antidiagonal Filter and the p₂ = e₁² − 2e₂ Identity
content:
The $k=2$ corollary applies `MvPolynomial.psum_eq_mul_esymm_sub_sum` at degree 2. The Mathlib recurrence gives: $p_2 = (-1)^3 \cdot 2 \cdot e_2 - \sum_{(a,b) \in \text{antidiag}(2),\, 0 < a < 2} (-1)^a e_a p_b$. The antidiagonal $\text{antidiag}(2) = \{(0,2), (1,1), (2,0)\}$; filtered to $0 < a < 2$ gives $\{(1,1)\}$. The proof computes this filter explicitly with `omega` to discharge membership conditions, giving: $p_2 = -2e_2 + e_1 \cdot p_1 = -2e_2 + e_1^2 = e_1^2 - 2e_2$ (using the $k=1$ result $p_1 = e_1$). The `ring` tactic closes the equality.

This identity $p_2 = e_1^2 - 2e_2$ is equivalent to $(\sum x_i)^2 = \sum x_i^2 + 2 \sum_{i<j} x_i x_j$ — the algebraic core of the AM-GM inequality for 2 variables and the parent's off-diagonal symmetry theorem.
mathContext: $\text{antidiag}(2) \cap \{(a,b) : 0 < a < 2\} = \{(1,1)\}$. Newton-Girard at $k=2$: $p_2 = -2e_2 - (-e_1 p_1) = e_1 p_1 - 2e_2 = e_1^2 - 2e_2$. In Lean: after `hfilt` proves the filter singleton via `omega`, `simp only [hfilt, Finset.sum_singleton, h1]` simplifies the sum, and `ring` closes the goal.

title: k=3 Corollary: Two-Element Antidiagonal and the p₃ Identity
content:
The $k=3$ corollary applies the same template as $k=2$ but with a two-element antidiagonal filter. The Newton-Girard recurrence at $k=3$ gives: $p_3 = 3e_3 - \sum_{(a,b) \in \text{antidiag}(3),\, 0 < a < 3} (-1)^a e_a p_b$. The filter $\{(a,b) : a+b=3, 0 < a < 3\} = \{(1,2), (2,1)\}$. The sum over this two-element set requires `Finset.sum_insert` to split the sum: $e_1 p_2 + (-e_2 p_1)$, after substituting the sign factors $(-1)^1 = -1$ and $(-1)^2 = 1$. The result: $p_3 = 3e_3 + e_1 p_2 - e_2 p_1$, closed by `ring`.

The `sum_insert (by decide : (1,2) ∉ ({(2,1)} : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)))` separates the two antidiagonal contributions. The `decide` tactic handles the finite membership check mechanically. The final `ring` folds all the sign arithmetic and algebraic simplifications automatically.
mathContext: $\text{antidiag}(3) \cap \{(a,b) : 0 < a < 3\} = \{(1,2), (2,1)\}$. Newton-Girard at $k=3$: $p_3 = 3e_3 - (-e_1 p_2 + e_2 p_1) = 3e_3 + e_1 p_2 - e_2 p_1$. In Lean: `Finset.sum_insert` splits the two-element finset sum; `ring` closes the identity after simplification.
